new_statements.quote: Grammatical morphemes did not have a tonal specification of their own. Nor were they pronounced with a fixed F0 pattern, as a neutral tone might be, or with less intensity. So an interpretation of the system as a combination of an initial stress with four tones, which would all be neutralized in suffixes, although considered for a moment, was rejected (Mazaudon 1973b:61-91). [...] a tendency to a less-than-one-tone-per-syllable structure is noted in languages with a weak syllable, like Burmese, and in some Chin dialects (Mazaudon 1977:76-90). These are also different from the Tamang type, where all syllables are evenly stressed.
new_statements.citation: Mazaudon, Martine. 2014. Studying emergent tone-systems in Nepal: Pitch, phonation and word-tone in Tamang. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 587-612.
new_statements.locator: p. 599 (sec. 5, word-tone) and p. 600 (sec. 6, typological considerations)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (text of the PDF we hold, LD&C 8, open access via HAL halshs-01118386 / hdl 10125/24617). Both halves of the quote are there verbatim: p. 599 (sec. 5 word-TONE), the text: 'Grammatical morphemes did not have a tonal specification of their own. Nor were they pronounced with a fixed F0 pattern, as a neutral tone might be, or with less intensity. So an interpretation of the system as a combination of an initial stress with four tones, which would all be neutralized in suffixes, although considered for a moment, was rejected (Mazaudon 1973b:61-91).' and p. 600 (sec. 6 SOME BRIEF TYPOLOGICAL CONSIDERATIONS), the text: '..a tendency to a less-than-one-tone-per-syllable structure is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tamang (Risiangku, Eastern Tamang) is a word-tone language: one of four lexical tone melodies (pitch + phonation) spreads over the whole phonological word (lexeme + suffixes); no syllable is singled out for stress — all syllables are described as evenly stressed, and an 'initial stress + tone' analysis was explicitly rejected. No stress-placement rule applies.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned (no stress prominence at all per the source).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Mazaudon 2005 adds that, unlike Lhasa Tibetan, Tamang inflectional suffixes are NOT de-stressed. Conflicting statements exist for other Tamang varieties: Yonjan-Tamang 1997 p. 21 (Sailung Eastern dialect, in Nepali) calls stress 'meaning-distinguishing' with minimal pairs that look like relabelled tone contrasts; Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970 p. 116 give fixed word-initial stress for Western Tamang (Nuwakot, tdg); Regmi 2019 p. 46 says stress is not distinctive in (Western) Tamang.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of tone (and of the 'evenly stressed' claim) is the phonological word = lexeme plus its string of suffixes; based on field elicitation and acoustic data from Risiangku (Eastern Tamang [taj]), the language into which tsf was merged; Mazaudon 2005 generalises 'roughly equal prominence of all syllables' to the whole TGTM group. Not based on data from the former Southwestern Tamang area.
new_statements.identity_note: sout2718 is a Glottolog 'Bookkeeping' entry: ISO 639-3 change request 2014-035 (SIL Nepal, adopted 2015-01-12) retired [tsf] Southwestern Tamang and merged it into [taj] Eastern Tamang (Glottolog east2347), citing Varenkamp 1997 and ~87% lexical similarity / ~87% intelligibility. Ethnologue 17 (2014) located tsf in southern Dhading, Chitwan, NW Makwanpur, Bara, Parsa, Rautahat and W/NW Kathmandu district. No phonology or grammar of a variety from that area was found. The quoted statement (Mazaudon 2014) describes Risiangku Tamang, an Eastern Tamang [taj] variety (east2347), and Mazaudon extends the 'evenly stressed / word-tone' characterisation to Tamang and the TGTM group as a whole. Note the dialect-geography ambiguity: Regmi 2019 (after Eppele et al. 2012) and Ajitman Tamang 2011 place NW Makwanpur / S Dhading / Chitwan / Bara-Parsa-Rautahat Tamang with WESTERN Tamang (tdg, west2415), for which Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970 state fixed initial stress. Because the code is retired and confers no separate identity, any catalog entry belongs under east2347 (or west2415), not under sout2718.

sources.citation: Mazaudon, Martine. 2005. On tone in Tamang and neighbouring languages: synchrony and diachrony. In S. Kaji (ed.), Proceedings of the Symposium Cross-linguistic Studies of Tonal Phenomena, 79-96. Tokyo: ILCAA (HAL halshs-00139489).
sources.note: HAL preprint p. 10-11 (sec. 2.3.1-2.3.2): 'Tamang syllables appear to be all about equally stressed'; Bodish languages 'do not generally give prominence, either by way of F0 or intensity, to one syllable per unit. Either all syllables have roughly equal prominence, as in the TGTM group, or one syllable per unit is weak.'

sources.citation: Hari, Maria, Doreen Taylor & Kenneth L. Pike. 1970. Tamang tone and higher levels. In A. Hale & K. L. Pike (eds), Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal, Part I (Occasional Papers of the Wolfenden Society 3), Urbana: University of Illinois. (Western Tamang, Sahugaon, Nuwakot = tdg/west2415).
sources.note: p. 116 sec. C 'Stress': 'In Western Tamang the basic word stress falls always on the first syllable of a word'; intonational stress on the last syllable before juncture can be intense; word stress manifested by consonant/vowel onset intensity and slight length, not pitch. Western Tamang, not the tsf area.

sources.citation: Regmi, Dan Raj. 2019. Coding grammatical signals in Western Tamang: a typological perspective. Nepalese Linguistics 34: 43-51.
sources.note: p. 46 sec. 3.7 'Intonation and stress': 'The stress is not distinctive in Tamang.' No placement. Notes (after Eppele et al. 2012) that Western Tamang [tdg] is spoken in NW Makwanpur (Phakel, Kulekhani, Markhu, Tistung, Palung) and N Kathmandu, i.e. part of the former tsf area; lists tsf among Tamang dialect codes.

sources.citation: Tamang, Ajitman. 2011. A sketch grammar of Tamang (Tamang as spoken in Bomtang, Nuwakot). 87 pp. Author's upload, archive.org.
sources.note: Silent on stress; sec. 3.5 'Tamang is classified as a tonal language', four tones (high, mid-high, mid, low). Sec. 2.5 defines a 'Western Tamang Dialect' covering Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, NW Makwanpur, Chitwan, Bara, Parsa, Rautahat (includes the former tsf area).

sources.citation: Yonjan Tamang, Amrit. 2054 BS [1997]. तामाङ व्याकरण (Tamang Vyakaran) [A grammar of Tamang, in Nepali]. Kathmandu: Nepal Rajakiya Pragya-Pratisthan (Royal Nepal Academy). Based on the Sailung (Eastern) dialect.
sources.note: p. 21 sec. 1.2.1 बलाघात (Stress): 'अक्षर वा शब्दमा बल पर्दा शब्द र वाक्यको अर्थमा भिन्नता हुन्छ। तामाङभाषामा बलाघात अर्थभेदक छ' = stress is meaning-distinguishing in Tamang, with pairs या 'hand' / या' 'is', तोजी 'beat' / तो'जी 'was needed' plus sentence-focus examples; sec. 1.2.4 gives four tones after Mazaudon. Native-speaker grammar of the Sailung/Eastern dialect (east2347); the 'stress' pairs look like relabelled tonal contrasts; conflicts with Mazaudon; no placement rule.
Nothing; records retirement of tsf, merged into Eastern Tamang [taj] effective 2015-01-12 (CR 2014-035); only reference is the ISO change request.
